title: “And how, monks, is a monk ‘one who has learned’? He has destroyed evil, unwholesome states that are defiling, leading to renewed existence, fearful, producing…
content: “And how, monks, is a monk ‘one who has learned’? He has destroyed evil, unwholesome states that are defiling, leading to renewed existence, fearful, producing painful results, leading to future birth, aging, and death. Thus, monks, a monk is ‘one who has learned.’”

title: “Monks, before my enlightenment, while I was still a bodhisatta, not yet fully enlightened, I thought: ‘What is the gratification, what is the peril, what…
content: “Monks, before my enlightenment, while I was still a bodhisatta, not yet fully enlightened, I thought: ‘What is the gratification, what is the peril, what is the escape in the case of form? … in the case of feeling? … perception? … formations? … consciousness?’ Then, monks, I thought: ‘The pleasure and joy that arise dependent on form — that is the gratification of form. That form is impermanent, suffering, subject to change — that is the peril of form. The removal and abandonment of desire and lust for form — that is the escape from form.’”

title: Elder Telakāni: I sank deep in a lake, Full of mud, unable to escape — Full of deceit, envy, Tension and darkness. Thunder of restlessness…
content:
Elder Telakāni:

I sank deep in a lake,
Full of mud, unable to escape —
Full of deceit, envy,
Tension and darkness.

Thunder of restlessness resounded,
Clouds of fetters covered,
Waterfall of wrong thoughts,
Connected with sensual desire —
They swept me away
Into the ocean of wrong views.

Everywhere, streams flow,
Creepers stand and sprout.
Who can block those streams?
Who can cut down the creepers?

Venerable sir, make a dam,
Block those streams.
Do not let the water
Born of mind sweep you away,
As a rapid current sweeps away a tree.

So I, afraid,
Seeking the far shore from this shore,
Then the Teacher,
Attended by the noble Saṅgha,
With the weapon of wisdom,
Waits as a support for people.

He brought me, while sinking,
A well-made ladder —
The Buddha, pure, firm,
Made of the heartwood of Dhamma —
Then he said to me:
“Do not be afraid!”

Climbing the tower of mindfulness,
From there I contemplate
People who delight in identity view —
Formerly, I was proud.

When I saw the path,
The boat I needed to board,
I did not abide in a self,
Seeing the supreme destination.

The dart that arises from self,
Born from the cause of existence —
He taught the supreme path,
The cessation of those things.

The knot that for a long time,
Hidden, lay within the skin —
The Buddha untied and threw it away,
Removing all that is harmful.

title: Elder Nun Sumedhā: Even if there were seventeen treasures, Filling the ten directions completely, Sensual desires are never satisfied — One dies, still unsatisfied. Sensual…
content:
Elder Nun Sumedhā:

Even if there were seventeen treasures,
Filling the ten directions completely,
Sensual desires are never satisfied —
One dies, still unsatisfied.

Sensual desires are like swords and spears,
Sensual desires are like a snake’s head,
Like a blazing torch,
Like a smooth-gnawed bone.

Sensual desires are not permanent,
Nor are they everlasting —
Much suffering, a great poison,
Like a red-hot iron ball —
The source of misfortune,
Resulting in suffering.

Sensual desires are like a fruit tree,
Like a piece of meat — trouble,
Like a dream, like a illusion —
Sensual desires are like borrowed goods.

Sensual desires are like swords, like stakes,
Disease and boils,
Misfortune and agitation —
Like a pit of glowing embers —
The source of misfortune,
Fear and destruction.

Fools, for a long time,
Weep in this wandering continuation.
From beginningless time until now,
They weep at being subject to death,
Weep for slain brothers,
Weep for being slain themselves.

Remember from beginningless time —
Tears, milk, and blood
Flow in saṃsāra,
Without ever stopping.
Remember the accumulation of bones
Of beings wandering on.

Remember the four oceans
Filled with tears, milk, and blood —
Remember the bones of one lifetime,
As high as Vepulla.

Remember from beginningless time —
Not enough to make
The whole Jambudīpa
As a heap of mustard seeds
Of mothers and fathers in saṃsāra.

Remember from beginningless time —
Grasses, trees, branches, leaves —
Not enough to contain
A four-fingered pot
For the fathers in saṃsāra.

Remember the image
Of the blind turtle in the eastern sea,
Poking its head into
The hole of a floating yoke —
To illustrate
How hard it is to be human.

title: Elder Māluṅkyaputta: Not lusting after forms, Seeing a form, mindful, The mind not clinging to the feeling, Not getting stuck, not remaining — As one…
content:
Elder Māluṅkyaputta:

Not lusting after forms,
Seeing a form, mindful,
The mind not clinging to the feeling,
Not getting stuck, not remaining —

As one sees a form,
Thus one feels the feeling —
Abandoning, not accumulating,
Mindful, practicing thus —

Thus, not storing up suffering,
He is said to be close to Nibbāna.

Not lusting after sounds,
Hearing a sound, mindful,
The mind not clinging to the feeling,
Not getting stuck, not remaining —

As one hears a sound,
Thus one feels the feeling —
Abandoning, not accumulating,
Mindful, practicing thus —
Thus, not storing up suffering,
He is said to be close to Nibbāna.

Not lusting after odors,
Smelling an odor, mindful,
The mind not clinging to the feeling,
Not getting stuck, not remaining —

As one smells an odor,
Thus one feels the feeling —
Abandoning, not accumulating,
Mindful, practicing thus —
Thus, not storing up suffering,
He is said to be close to Nibbāna.

Not lusting after tastes,
Tasting a flavor, mindful,
The mind not clinging to the feeling,
Not getting stuck, not remaining —

As one tastes a flavor,
Thus one feels the feeling —
Abandoning, not accumulating,
Mindful, practicing thus —
Thus, not storing up suffering,
He is said to be close to Nibbāna.

Not lusting after touches,
Feeling a touch, mindful,
The mind not clinging to the feeling,
Not getting stuck, not remaining —

As one feels a touch,
Thus one feels the feeling —
Abandoning, not accumulating,
Mindful, practicing thus —
Thus, not storing up suffering,
He is said to be close to Nibbāna.

Not lusting after phenomena,
Cognizing a phenomenon, mindful,
The mind not clinging to the feeling,
Not getting stuck, not remaining —

As one cognizes a phenomenon,
Thus one feels the feeling —
Abandoning, not accumulating,
Mindful, practicing thus —
Thus, not storing up suffering,
He is said to be close to Nibbāna.

title: “Venerable sir, how does future rebirth occur?” “Venerable sir, when beings are shrouded by ignorance and bound by craving, delighting here and there, thus future…
content: “Venerable sir, how does future rebirth occur?” “Venerable sir, when beings are shrouded by ignorance and bound by craving, delighting here and there, thus future rebirth occurs.” “Venerable sir, how does future rebirth not occur?” “Venerable sir, when ignorance is abandoned, knowledge arises, and craving is destroyed, thus future rebirth does not occur.”

title: “And what, monks, is non-restraint? Monks, there are forms cognizable by the eye that are desirable, agreeable, pleasant, charming, connected with sensuality, enticing. If a…
content: “And what, monks, is non-restraint? Monks, there are forms cognizable by the eye that are desirable, agreeable, pleasant, charming, connected with sensuality, enticing. If a monk delights in those forms, praises them, and dwells with lust for them, then that monk, monks, should understand: ‘I have fallen away from wholesome states.’ The Tathāgata calls this ‘falling away.’ … There are sounds cognizable by the ear … odors … tastes … touches … There are phenomena cognizable by the mind that are desirable … enticing. If a monk delights in those phenomena, praises them, and dwells with lust for them, then that monk should understand: ‘I have fallen away from wholesome states.’ The Tathāgata calls this ‘falling away.’ Thus, monks, is non-restraint.”

title: “Migajāla, there are forms cognizable by the eye that are desirable … enticing. If a monk does not delight in them, does not praise them,…
content: “Migajāla, there are forms cognizable by the eye that are desirable … enticing. If a monk does not delight in them, does not praise them, and dwells without lust for them — then delight ceases. Migajāla, I say that with the cessation of delight, suffering ceases. Sounds … Odors … Tastes … Touches … Migajāla, there are phenomena cognizable by the mind … If a monk does not delight in them, does not praise them, and dwells without lust for them — then delight ceases. Migajāla, I say that with the cessation of delight, suffering ceases.”

title: “One who indulges in sexual intercourse, Forgetting the teaching, Falls into wrong conduct — That life is not noble. One who formerly lived alone, Now…
content:
“One who indulges in sexual intercourse,
Forgetting the teaching,
Falls into wrong conduct —
That life is not noble.

One who formerly lived alone,
Now falls into sexual intercourse —
Like a swerving chariot,
He is called a worldling, a low person.

The good reputation he once had
He now loses.
Seeing this, one should train
To abandon sexual intercourse.

Overcome by thoughts,
He broods like a poor man —
Hearing others’ reproach,
He becomes dejected.

Then he makes weapons,
Attacked by others’ words —
He becomes greatly greedy,
Grasping at false speech.

Called wise, living alone,
If he falls into sexual intercourse,
He sorrows like a fool.

Seeing this danger,
The sage, steadfast before and after,
Lives solitary,
Not practicing sexual intercourse.

Train in seclusion —
This is the supreme noble practice.
Do not think yourself best,
Though you are close to Nibbāna.

The sage’s way is empty,
Not wishing for sensuality.
The one who has crossed the flood,
Envied and desired by people
Bound by sensual pleasures.”

title: “Monks, form is impermanent. What is impermanent is suffering. What is suffering is not-self. What is not-self should be seen as it actually is with…
content:
“Monks, form is impermanent. What is impermanent is suffering. What is suffering is not-self. What is not-self should be seen as it actually is with correct wisdom: ‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self.’ Feeling … perception … formations … consciousness is impermanent. What is impermanent is suffering. What is suffering is not-self. What is not-self should be seen as it actually is with correct wisdom: ‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self.’ Seeing thus, monks, a well-taught noble disciple becomes disenchanted with form … with feeling … with perception … with formations … with consciousness. Being disenchanted, he becomes dispassionate. Through dispassion, he is liberated. In liberation, knowledge arises: ‘Liberated.’ He knows: ‘Birth is destroyed, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more of this state of being.’

Happy indeed are the arahants,
In them no craving is found,
Conceit has been cut off,
The net of delusion is torn apart.

They have attained the imperturbable,
Their minds are far from defilement,
They are not stained in the world —
The holy ones, free from defilements.

Fully understanding the five aggregates,
Practicing the seven good qualities,
Praised by true persons,
Disciples of the Buddha.

Possessing seven treasures,
Completed in the three trainings,
The great heroes wander forth,
Having abandoned all fear.

Endowed with ten powers,
The great elephant is concentrated,
They are supreme in the world,
Craving has been destroyed.

Achieved the knowledge of the adept,
This body is their last,
The end of the holy life,
Achieved independently.

Not shaken by perceptions,
Liberated from renewed existence,
Having reached the tamed state,
They are conquerors in the world.

Above, below, and across,
They have no delight,
They roar the lion’s roar —
The supreme Buddhas in the world!
